newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt stumbles in local vote, League drubbed.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt stumbles in local vote, League drubbed.

text.p: Italy's centre-left coalition trailed in mayoral races in the key northern cities of Milan and Turin on Monday after local elections that strengthened the hand of the hard left party the government relies on to survive.
Sunday's elections in more than 1,100 towns and cities represented the first big test of support since Prime Minister Romano Prodi and his Olive Tree coalition won a general election a year ago.

They took place amid rising resentment at the high tax burden weighing on Italians as Prodi struggles to reduce Italy's budget deficit sufficiently to haul the country into the founding group for Europe's planned single currency.

The big loser was the Northern League, with the elections confirming a slump in support since its firebrand leader switched last year from a federalist to openly secessionist agenda for Italy's affluent north.

It lost control of Milan, Italy's business capital and second city, where outgoing mayor Marco Formentini finished a poor third, and was ousted from power from the three provincial governments it had previously run.

With most of the results in, the opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance secured a first round lead in the battles for mayors in the prize cities of Milan and Turin, pushing Olive Tree candidates into second place.
Both contests go to second round run-offs on May 11.
The hard left Communist Refoundation, which ensures the government its parliamentary majority, was the only party in the contests to boost its share of the vote significantly.

It indicated that it could seek a high price for backing Olive Tree candidates in second round voting in Milan, Turin and elsewhere in what could signal a rough ride ahead for Prodi as his government confronts crucial welfare reforms.

The party, opposed to any cuts in social spending, ran alone in both Milan and Turin, securing around 10 percent of the vote, and reaped 12 percent of votes in elections for six provincial administrations, up from 9.4 percent at the general election.
"Given that we got so many votes, this will give more importance to both our social spending and structural reform position," party leader Fausto Bertinotti told Reuters.
About one-fifth of Italy's national electorate was eligible to vote in Sunday's elections.

The Olive Tree took the lead in mayoral races in the northeastern cities of Trieste and Pordenone, in the Adriatic port of Ancona and in Reggio Calabria on the toe of Italy. It also led in two of the six elections for the president of provincial governments and won one outright.
But political analysts and the opposition said the overall Refoundation performance had underlined that the government could not win a national election without the hard left.

"The Olive Tree does not represent a majority on its own in Italy," right-wing politician Gianfranco Fini said. "It looks likely that Bertinotti will raise the price of his cooperation with the Olive Tree from tomorrow."
Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, whose centrist Italian Renewal party won hardly any votes, said in Washington that he would not be held hostage to Refoundation.

Raising the heat in the imminent battle on welfare reform, he told a World Economic Laboratory conference that structural measures to cut spending, including on pensions, had to be taken even if that meant breaking Prodi's parliamentary majority.

"If the extreme left and the trade unions continue to oppose spending cuts or any change in the welfare state, the government must take the initiative and submit a bill to parliament for which it will be possible to obtain the support of the opposition," Dini said.
